stages.title: Renaissance and Scientific Revolution
stages.hook: In 1543 two books were published: one placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre of the planets, and one corrected the human anatomy taught for 1,400 years. Why did new ways of looking at the world appear then?
explain: The Renaissance, from about the 1300s in Italian cities such as Florence, was a revival of interest in classical learning, art and human potential. It was paid for by wealthy merchants and fed by texts and scholars from Byzantium and the Islamic world. Artists such as Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo studied nature closely.
Printing helped. Movable-type printing existed earlier in China and Korea, and Gutenberg developed a press in Germany around 1450. Books became cheaper and ideas spread faster.

The Scientific Revolution followed. Copernicus (1543) argued for a Sun-centred model; Vesalius (1543) based anatomy on dissection; Galileo used a telescope from 1609; and Newton's Principia (1687) explained motion and gravity with mathematics. The key change was testing ideas with observation and experiment instead of relying on authority.

example.q: Why did the printing press speed up science?
steps: Hand-copied books were slow and costly, and copying could add errors.
Printing produced many identical copies cheaply.
Scholars in different places could check and build on the same results.
example.a: Cheap, identical copies let ideas be shared and checked.

analogies.tech: Printing did for knowledge what the internet does now: it multiplied copies and cut costs.
analogies.city: Italian cities competed to attract the best artists, like cities hosting a famous festival.
analogies.sea: Better navigation tools, like the telescope and charts, helped sailors and scientists.

stages.mnemonic: Print, patrons, observe, test: four engines of the Renaissance and the Scientific Revolution.
terms: A European revival of art and learning from the 14th to 17th centuries.
A shift to explaining nature by observation, experiment and mathematics.
A person who pays artists or scholars.

misc.wrong: Europe alone produced the Scientific Revolution.
misc.right: It drew on Greek, Islamic, Indian and Chinese knowledge, and on global trade, while new work in Europe followed.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: historians debate whether 'Revolution' fits a slow change. Copernicus's tools resemble those of earlier astronomers such as Ibn al-Shatir, and how directly he used them is debated.

stages.title: Reformation and major religious transformations
stages.hook: In 1517 a monk in a small German town published a list of arguments about church practice. Within a century, Europe's religious map had changed. How could one list matter so much?
explain: In 1517 Martin Luther published his Ninety-five Theses, criticising the sale of indulgences. Printing spread his arguments quickly. Others, such as John Calvin, developed different Protestant teachings. In England, Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 through the Act of Supremacy, partly for political reasons.

The Catholic Church responded with reforms at the Council of Trent (1545 to 1563). Conflicts followed. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let German rulers choose Lutheran or Catholic worship in their lands, and the Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) ended with the Peace of Westphalia.

Religious change was global in this period. In 1501 the Safavid dynasty made Twelver Shi'a Islam the state religion of Iran. In Punjab, Guru Nanak founded Sikhism around 1500. The Mughal emperor Akbar (ruled 1556 to 1605) held discussions among religions in his court.

example.q: Why did printing matter to Luther's movement?
steps: Pamphlets could be printed cheaply in large numbers.
They could be read in German, not just Latin.
So ideas spread far beyond his town.
example.a: Printing spread his ideas widely in local languages.

analogies.tech: Pamphlets then were like viral posts now.
analogies.city: A town council could choose a church's form, much like voting a local rule.
analogies.home: Families sometimes split by faith, as a household can disagree about a rule.

terms: A 16th century movement to reform the Western Church that created Protestant churches.
A Church grant reducing punishment for sin, which became controversial when sold.
A Christian who belongs to a church formed in the Reformation.
A split in a religious community.

misc.wrong: The Reformation was only about belief.
misc.right: It also involved politics, power, money, language and printing.

stages.limits: Documented fact: dates and treaties. Scholarly uncertainty: historians debate how far politics or sincere belief drove each ruler.

stages.title: Age of global maritime exploration
stages.hook: When Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498, he found busy ports and a pilot from East Africa who knew the route. What does this say about who 'discovered' the Indian Ocean?
explain: Between about 1400 and 1600 ships linked all the oceans. Chinese fleets under Zheng He sailed to East Africa from 1405 to 1433. Portugal explored down the African coast; Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape in 1488, and Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in India in 1498.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, reached the Caribbean, islands long home to Indigenous peoples. Ferdinand Magellan's expedition (1519 to 1522) was the first to sail around the world, though Magellan died in the Philippines and Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the voyage.

Europeans were not discovering empty seas. Indian Ocean traders, Polynesian navigators and Arab, Indian and African pilots already knew many routes. The new links brought the Columbian Exchange: maize, potatoes and tomatoes spread to the Old World, and horses, wheat and diseases to the Americas, with devastating results for Indigenous peoples.

example.q: Why is 'discovery' a debatable word for Columbus's voyage?
steps: The Americas had been home to millions of people for thousands of years.
What changed in 1492 was sustained contact with Europe.
So 'arrival' or 'contact' is more accurate.
example.a: The land was already inhabited; the new thing was contact.

analogies.sea: Monsoon-based Indian Ocean trade had a regular rhythm that da Gama joined.
analogies.tech: The caravel and the magnetic compass were the new technology of the day.
analogies.farm: Potatoes from the Andes later fed growing populations in Europe and Asia.

terms: A small, manoeuvrable sailing ship used by Portuguese explorers.

Sailing all the way around the world.
A person who guides ships through waters they know.

misc.wrong: Europeans discovered the oceans and the Americas.
misc.right: Indigenous peoples and Indian Ocean mariners already knew these lands and seas; Europeans made new, lasting connections.

stages.limits: Documented fact: voyages and dates. Scholarly uncertainty: death toll from disease in the Americas is estimated, not measured exactly.

stages.title: Colonialism, slavery and resistance
stages.hook: Between the 1500s and 1860s, millions of Africans were taken across the Atlantic against their will. How was this system built, and how did people resist it?
explain: From the 1500s, European powers established colonies in the Americas, Africa and Asia. The colonies often depended on forced labour. The transatlantic slave trade carried more than 12 million Africans in ships, and about 10.7 million survived the Middle Passage. Enslaved people worked on plantations producing sugar, tobacco and cotton, and in mines. Slavery also existed in other forms elsewhere, including trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean trades.

People resisted in many ways: by daily acts of refusal, by escaping to maroon communities such as Palmares in Brazil, and by rebellion. Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba resisted Portuguese expansion in the 1600s. The Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) led to Haiti's independence on 1 January 1804, the first state founded after a successful uprising of enslaved people.

Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of its empire in 1833, with compensation paid to owners, not the enslaved. Abolition came from the resistance of enslaved people and campaigns by many, including formerly enslaved writers such as Olaudah Equiano.

example.q: Why was the Haitian Revolution so significant?
steps: Enslaved people overthrew a colonial slave society.
They founded a new state in 1804.
It challenged the idea that slavery was permanent and inspired others.
example.a: It showed enslaved people could win freedom and form a state.

analogies.sea: The Middle Passage was a deadly crossing; survivors' accounts are key sources.
analogies.farm: Plantations were like large factories in fields, built on forced labour.
analogies.city: Port cities like Liverpool, Lisbon and Salvador grew in this trade, and its legacies remain.

terms: The forced shipping of enslaved Africans to the Americas.
A settlement of escaped enslaved people.
A large farm growing cash crops with forced labour.

misc.right: They resisted constantly, through escape, rebellion, culture and law.

stages.limits: Documented fact: voyage records show the scale. Scholarly uncertainty: numbers for trans-Saharan and Indian Ocean slave trades are less certain.

stages.title: Enlightenment and revolutionary movements
stages.hook: In 1776 a declaration said 'all men are created equal', yet many signers held enslaved people. How can ideals and practice conflict?
explain: The Enlightenment (roughly 1685 to 1789) was an intellectual movement in Europe that stressed reason, individual rights and questioning authority. John Locke wrote of natural rights and government by consent. Montesquieu argued for separating powers. Voltaire defended free speech, and Rousseau wrote about the people's will. Kant urged people to 'dare to know' for themselves. Many Enlightenment ideas also drew on wider exchanges, including discussions about Chinese and Islamic societies.

Ideas inspired revolutions. The American Declaration of Independence (1776) broke from British rule. In France, the revolution of 1789 produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Olympe de Gouges answered in 1791 with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen. In Haiti, enslaved people claimed those rights for themselves.
The reality was uneven. Rights were often limited by gender, race, class and property, and Enlightenment thinkers disagreed on slavery and empire.

example.q: Why did the claim that 'all men are equal' clash with slavery?
steps: The statement set a universal principle.
Slavery denied that principle to a group of people.
Critics, including enslaved people, pointed out the contradiction.
example.a: Universal ideals were applied to few, creating a contradiction.

analogies.sport: Rules that apply to every player are fair; rules that exempt some players are not.
analogies.city: Separation of powers is like having a mayor, a council and a court check each other.
analogies.music: A revolution is like a new rhythm that changes how everyone plays.

terms: A movement stressing reason, rights and questioning authority.
An idea that government rests on an agreement with the governed.
Dividing government among branches that check each other.
A fundamental, often rapid, change of government or society.

misc.wrong: Enlightenment ideals were applied equally to everyone.
misc.right: They were often limited; excluded groups argued for their extension.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: historians debate how far ideas caused revolutions rather than economic and political pressures.

stages.title: Industrial Revolution
stages.hook: In 1750 most British people lived in the countryside. By 1850 about half lived in towns. What made so many people move?
explain: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain from around 1760. Factories using machines and steam power replaced much hand production. Spinning machines and power looms transformed cotton cloth. James Watt's improvements to the steam engine from 1769 made it far more efficient. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830.

Factories drew workers to growing cities. Work was long and often dangerous, and children worked in mills. Laws such as the Factory Act of 1833 began to limit child labour. Trade unions and reform movements grew.

The revolution was linked to the wider world: raw cotton was often grown by enslaved people in the Americas, and Indian handloom industries were hurt by competition. Industrialisation then spread to Belgium, the United States, Germany and, after the Meiji Restoration of 1868, Japan. It also began the large-scale burning of coal, which increased carbon dioxide in the air.

example.q: Why did cotton mills need coal and steam?
steps: Machines needed power beyond human muscles.
Steam engines burned coal to turn machinery anywhere, not only beside rivers.
So factories could be built near towns and workers.
example.a: Steam power freed factories from rivers and concentrated production.

analogies.farm: Machines doing the work of many hands is like a combine harvester replacing a field of reapers.
analogies.city: Rapid growth created crowded housing and the need for sewers.
analogies.tech: Railways were the era's internet: they sped up goods and news.

terms: The shift to machine and factory production, beginning in Britain.

An organisation of workers seeking better pay and conditions.
A law regulating working conditions in factories.

misc.wrong: The Industrial Revolution happened only in Britain and benefited everyone.
misc.right: It spread worldwide, and it brought benefits and harms unevenly, including harsh labour and links to slavery and colonial trade.

stages.limits: Scholarly uncertainty: historians debate why Britain industrialised first, weighing coal, capital, colonial trade and institutions.

stages.title: African, Asian and American independence movements
stages.hook: In 1896 an African army defeated a European army at Adwa and secured its independence. How did peoples across the world resist and end foreign rule before 1900?
explain: Independence movements began in the Americas. After the Haitian Revolution (1804), Spanish America rose in the 1810s and 1820s. Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led forces that freed much of South America; Mexico became independent in 1821 and Brazil in 1822. Creoles often led these states, while Indigenous and enslaved peoples were not always freed or given equal rights.

In Africa, Ethiopia under Emperor Menelik II defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896, and remained independent. In Asia, India saw the rising of 1857 against the East India Company, and the Indian National Congress formed in 1885. Japan avoided colonisation through the Meiji reforms of 1868.
Movements took many forms: armed revolt, petitions, newspapers, strikes and cultural revival. Each was shaped by local conditions.

stages.title: European and global imperial history
stages.hook: In 1884-85 diplomats met in Berlin to set rules for claiming African territory, and no African ruler was present. How did empires reshape the world?
explain: Empires have existed on every continent, including the Mughal, Ottoman, Qing and Russian empires. In the 1800s European powers, and later the United States and Japan, expanded rapidly. The British ruled India directly from 1858. After the Opium Wars, China's Treaty of Nanking (1842) ceded Hong Kong to Britain and opened ports.

The Berlin Conference (1884 to 1885) set rules for claims in Africa, and by 1914 European powers controlled most of the continent, with Ethiopia and Liberia the main exceptions. In the Congo Free State (1885 to 1908), King Leopold II's regime caused great suffering, and international outcry forced Belgium to take over.

Empires moved goods, ideas and people, including railways, schools and languages. But they imposed unequal rule and extracted resources. People resisted and also negotiated, and colonial borders still shape modern states.

stages.title: Antarctic expeditions and polar science
stages.hook: Two teams raced to the South Pole in 1911-12; one returned safely, one did not. What did the expeditions achieve for science, apart from the race?
explain: Antarctica has no Indigenous population, so its modern history is one of expeditions and science. In 1839 to 1843 James Clark Ross sailed into what is now the Ross Sea. The Belgica expedition (1897 to 1899) was the first to spend a winter in the Antarctic region, and the Southern Cross expedition (1898 to 1900) was the first to winter on the mainland.

In the Heroic Age (about 1897 to 1922), Robert Falcon Scott's Discovery expedition (1901 to 1904) and Ernest Shackleton's Nimrod expedition (1907 to 1909) explored inland. Roald Amundsen's team reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911. Scott's party arrived on 17 January 1912 and died on the return journey.

Scientists on these expeditions measured weather and magnetism, collected fossils and rocks, and studied animals such as emperor penguins. Findings of fossil plants helped to show that Antarctica was once part of a warmer supercontinent. Later, the International Geophysical Year of 1957-58 and the Antarctic Treaty of 1959 turned the continent into a place for international research.

example.q: Why did expeditions bring scientists as well as explorers?
steps: Little was known about the continent's weather, rocks and life.
Measurements from many places over a long time were needed.
Scientists could collect samples and record data while there.
example.a: To gather data and samples that could only be obtained there.
